HONORING DR. LEE MERRIAM
TALBOT

HON. MIKE THOMPSON
OF CALIFORNIA

rfrederick on LAP6701GR3PROD with REMARKS

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Mr. THOMPSON of California. Mr. Speaker,
I rise today to honor Dr. Lee Merriam Talbot,
a world renowned environmentalist who dedicated his life and career to conservation.
Dr. Talbot was born in 1930 in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Dr. Talbot holds an Associate of Arts degree, a Bachelor of Arts in
liberal arts and wildlife ecology, a Master of
Science in vertebrate ecology, and a Ph.D. in
geography and ecology, all from the University
of California, Berkeley.
Dr. Talbot was one of the most influential
wildlife conservation scientists and environmental policy architects of the 20th century.
Dr. Talbot helped advance the scientific idea
that ecosystems must be protected as whole
systems, not simply individual species. This
later became central to the study of modern
conservation biology. He was the primary architect and author of numerous environmentally focused objectives including the landmark Endangered Species Act (ESA), the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), the Convention on Trade of Endangered Species
(CITES), and the World Heritage Convention.
Dr. Talbot advised on environmental issues in
over 130 countries, working closely with the
World Wildlife Fund, United Nations, and the
International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Through these efforts, Dr. Talbot became
internationally known for his major ecological
fieldwork and research that resulted in the creation of the Serengeti National Park, the
Masai Mara National Reserve, and many more
World Heritage Sites.
Dr. Talbot was the Senior Scientist and Director of International Affairs of the Council on
Environmental Quality (CEQ) in the West
Wing of the White House for President Nixon,
President Ford, and President Carter. In this
position, he placed endangered species high
on the Nation’s political and environmental
agenda. His efforts resulted in the Endangered
Species Act, one of the most important envi-

VerDate Sep 11 2014

08:02 Nov 11, 2026

E1185

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

Jkt 079060

ronmental pieces of legislation in United
States history, getting signed into law by
President Nixon on December 28, 1973.
Thanks to Dr. Talbot, the ESA has helped prevent the extinction of species such as the Bald
Eagle, Gray Whale, Peregrine Falcon, California Condor, American Alligator, and countless other animals.
Dr. Talbot was also a beloved professor at
George Mason University, where he taught
environmental science, public policy, conversation biology, and international affairs for
nearly 30 years. Dr. Talbot served in the
United States Marine Corps during the Korean
War. He was also a Resident Ecologist at the
Smithsonian Institution and a championship
racecar driver for seven decades. His last race
took place when he was 87 years old, at Laguna Seca raceway in Monterey, California,
one of the largest and most prestigious motor
sports events in the world. At this race, Dr.
Talbot received the prestigious Spirit of Monterey Award.
Dr. Talbot’s father, Murrell Williams Talbot,
a noted ecologist, was closely tied to the early
conservation movement in California. Dr. Talbot’s wife, Martha ‘‘Marty’’ Hayne Talbot,
spent much of her youth growing up in St.
Helena. Dr. Talbot and his wife strongly encouraged organically farming their Napa Valley
Zinfandel vineyard before this was widely
practiced in the valley. Their children, Lawrence Hayne Talbot and Russell Merriam Talbot, took responsibility for farming their family
vineyards in 2008. To this day, the Talbot family vineyard is one of the oldest family-held
vineyard properties in Napa.
Mr. Speaker, Dr. Talbot was described as a

figures of the 20th century will live on in his
former students, the environmental laws he
guided into reality, and the wildlife and wild
places he fiercely protected throughout his life.
Therefore, it is fitting and proper that we honor
him here today.

Mr. GOSAR. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to
recognize and congratulate the City of Goodyear, Arizona, for its 80th anniversary as an
incorporated community.
The story and history of Goodyear is
uniquely Arizonan: originally purchased by
President Paul W. Litchfield of the Goodyear
Tire & Rubber Company in 1917, Goodyear
began its life as a small community built
around a 16,000-acre Egyptian long-fiber cotton farm. This farm would not only help remedy cotton shortages during the First World
War; it would help produce fabric meshes for
Goodyear’s 1918 Pneumatic Cord Tire—the
first widely produced pneumatic tire in the
world.
During the Second World War, Goodyear
played another important role in Arizona’s
wider efforts to support America’s struggle
against tyranny; Goodyear hosted the Naval
Air Facility, an auxiliary airfield for Luke

E:\CR\FM\A10NO8.027

E10NOPT1

E1186

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

Airforce Base, and an aircraft manufacturing
plant that provided crucial parts for the B–29
Superfortress and other iconic bombers.
These early chapters in Goodyear’s history established the town’s traditions of hard work, innovation, patriotism, and perseverance. After
the war ended, Goodyear was finally incorporated on November 16, 1946.
At the time, Goodyear, Arizona only consisted of 151 homes, 250 apartments, and a
handful of local businesses catering to the
nearby airfields and manufacturing plant. But
with eight decades of sustained growth, Goodyear has flourished; slowly becoming one of
Arizona’s most dynamic communities with approximately 125,000 residents. Goodyear is a
proud part of Phoenix’s West Valley, providing
prosperity, opportunity, beauty, and hope to all
who call the Valley of the Sun their home.
Since 1985, Goodyear has been one of Arizona’s major cities. Since Goodyear was designated an official city, generations of families,
entrepreneurs, farmers, veterans, workers,
and community leaders have worked together
to shape its continued success going into the
future.
As the proud Representative of Goodyear in
Arizona’s 9th Congressional District, I am honored to recognize this important milestone.
The city’s continued growth and prosperity are
a true testament not only to the time, talents,
and energy of those who built it; it is a testament to Goodyear’s belief that all Arizonans
must work together to make Arizona the greatest state in our great Nation.
I extend my sincere congratulations to
Mayor Joe Pizzillo, the members of Goodyear
City Council, all city employees, community organizations, local businesses, and, most importantly, to the citizens of Goodyear on 80
years of achievement.
May the next 80 years bring continued opportunity, prosperity, and success to this blossoming Arizona community. Happy 80th anniversary, Goodyear.

HON. TROY A. CARTER

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to humbly honor and celebrate the
heroic courage and commitment of New Orleans Police Officer Christian Beyer. Officer
Beyer has served the citizens of New Orleans,
Louisiana since 2024. He currently serves in
the 5th District Unit.
On Wednesday, January 1, 2025, a man
drove a pickup into crowds celebrating the
New Year on Bourbon Street early killing 14
people. President Biden said he was ‘‘inspired
by ISIS.’’ This unfortunate event occurred near

PO 00000

Frm 00010

Fmt 0626

Sfmt 9920

November 10, 2026

the intersection of Canal and Bourbon Streets
in the city’s historic French Quarter, the heart
of the Louisiana tourism industry and a driver
of the state’s economy. This attack was clearly
intended to harm many more people. This terrorist used a 6,000-pound truck as a weapon
and then opened fire. He had planted explosives, which he intended to detonate.
He sped his rented truck around a police
car that was blocking an entrance to Bourbon
Street at about 3:15 a.m. Wednesday morning
and struck several people along the street before crashing the truck into an obstacle setup
in the street. He then opened fire and died in
a shootout with police. Two of those injured in
the attack were police officers. Investigators
confirmed they found what appeared to be improvised explosive devices in the truck.
‘‘This man was trying to run over as many
people as he possibly could,’’ the New Orleans police superintendent, Anne Kirkpatrick,
said in a news conference Wednesday. ‘‘He
was hellbent on creating the carnage and the
damage that he did.’’
The actions of Officer Christian Beyer, and
his fellow officers on New Year’s Day highlight
the profound impact of the NOPD’s dedication
to public safety. His teamwork, professionalism, and courage under fire are a reminder of the daily sacrifices made by law enforcement officers to protect the lives of others.
The officers didn’t have a chance to make
actual tactical decisions amongst themselves.
They acted as a team. Some of these men
and women didn’t work together ever before,
many from different jurisdictions and departments. But the individual officers who were
closer to the scene, who acted on a threat and
eliminated the threat, did everything that you
would expect them to do and more, especially
under the circumstances. At least 57 others
were injured, including two police officers who
were shot.
Throughout numerous interviews, each of
them expressed the same sentiment—they
were simply doing what they believed was expected of them when they joined the New Orleans Police Department. Officer Christian
Beyer’s bravery is a testament to his character
and his commitment to serving and protecting
this city and its visitors.
The only reason there wasn’t a greater loss
of life was because of the quick work of the
New Orleans Police Department. We have all
heard stories of police officers and responders
in other cities freezing in the face of a crisis—
not Officer Beyer. He ran to danger and quickly neutralized it before the attacker could
cause more harm. For this reason, I recognize
Officer Christian Beyer, a true hero saving
countless lives. I humbly thank him for his
courageous efforts and unwavering service as
a member of the New Orleans Police Department.

HONORING CHARLIE TOLEDO

HON. MIKE THOMPSON
OF CALIFORNIA

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Mr. THOMPSON of California. Mr. Speaker,
I rise today to honor Charlie Toledo, in recognition of her over 40 years of expertise and
advocacy in social justice.
Charlie Toledo was born in 1950 in Albuquerque, New Mexico, as a twin in a family of
10 children. She attended a Catholic high
school with deep philosophies which taught
her how to question, research, and work hard.
After college, she began fighting against the
draft in Orange County. She was a lifelong
learner and continued to study, work, and research throughout her life.
Charlie worked as the Executive Director
and founder of the Suscol Intertribal Council
from 1992, located in Napa County. She went
on to work on the National Water Board in
San Francisco and became the Chair of the
Women’s Intercultural Network. She additionally worked on the Advisory Committee for the
California Rural Indian Health Board (CRIHB)
and assisted in the movement to reclaim tobacco as medicine. Charlie’s contributions to
the community include her extensive experience as a community organizer in regional,
statewide, national, and international forums.
Since 1982, she has worked in alternative
healthcare fields, as well as background in
mediation for individuals, families, and organizations. She would speak out politically for
water, forest, and soil management when it
was unsafe to do so as an Indigenous woman.
In her over three decades of public service,
Charlie created and taught an historical trauma education model to educate people about
our Indigenous community. She also facilitated
a community mural in remembrance of the Indigenous people of Napa. She has been an
avid component of the cultural exchange with
Mexico and the Tuspan people and has been
an organic gardener since 1978. Charlie was
a midwife before it was legal to have home
births, advocating for a more humane birthing
system in the State of California.
Charlie Toledo leaves behind a legacy of Indigenous leadership, humanitarian advocacy,
and deep cultural reconnection that continues
to inspire and guide communities worldwide.
Mr. Speaker, Charlie Toledo has dedicated
her life to protecting the Indigenous people
and underrepresented communities in California and the United States of America. She
has transformed the lives of those around her
through her service and mentorship to others.
Therefore, it is fitting and proper that we honor
her here today.

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to humbly honor and celebrate the
heroic courage and commitment of New Orleans Police Officer Joseph Rodrigue. Officer
Rodrigue has served the citizens of New Orleans, Louisiana for 10 years. He currently
serves as a Senior Police Officer in the 3rd
District Unit.
On Wednesday, January 1, 2025, a man
drove a pickup into crowds celebrating the
New Year on Bourbon Street early killing 14
people. President Biden said he was ‘‘inspired
by ISIS.’’ This unfortunate event occurred near
the intersection of Canal and Bourbon Streets
in the city’s historic French Quarter, the heart
of the Louisiana tourism industry and a driver
of the state’s economy. This attack was clearly
intended to harm many more people. This terrorist used a 6,000-pound truck as a weapon
and then opened fire. He had planted explosives, which he intended to detonate.
He sped his rented truck around a police
car that was blocking an entrance to Bourbon
Street at about 3:15 a.m. Wednesday morning
and struck several people along the street before crashing the truck into an obstacle setup
in the street. He then opened fire and died in
a shootout with police. Two of those injured in
the attack were police officers. Investigators
confirmed they found what appeared to be improvised explosive devices in the truck.
‘‘This man was trying to run over as many
people as he possibly could,’’ the New Orleans police superintendent, Anne Kirkpatrick,
said in a news conference Wednesday. ‘‘He
was hellbent on creating the carnage and the
damage that he did.’’
The actions of Officer Joseph Rodrigue and
his fellow officers on New Year’s Day highlight
the profound impact of the NOPD’s dedication
to public safety. His teamwork, professionalism, and courage under fire are a reminder of the daily sacrifices made by law enforcement officers to protect the lives of others.
The officers didn’t have a chance to make
actual tactical decisions amongst themselves.
They acted as a team. Some of these men
and women didn’t work together ever before,
many from different jurisdictions and departments. But the individual officers who were
closer to the scene, who acted on a threat and
eliminated the threat, did everything that you
would expect them to do and more, especially
under the circumstances. At least 57 others
were injured, including Officer Rodrigue, receiving a gunshot wound to his left leg, requiring multiple surgeries. Another police officer
was wounded and is also recovering from his
injuries.
Throughout numerous interviews, each of
them expressed the same sentiment—they
were simply doing what they believed was expected of them when they joined the New Orleans Police Department. Officer Joseph
Rodrigue’s bravery is a testament to his character and his commitment to serving and protecting this city and its visitors.

HONORING CLAY LACY ON RECEIVING THE KANSAS AVIATION MUSEUM’S LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT
AWARD

HON. RON ESTES
OF KANSAS

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Mr. ESTES. Mr. Speaker, I rise to honor
Clay Lacy, a native of Wichita, and one of the
most accomplished aviators in American history. Tonight, the Kansas Aviation Museum
will present him with the Lifetime Achievement
Award in recognition for his extraordinary contributions to aviation around the world.
Nearly a century ago, in 1928, Wichita was
designated as the Air Capital of the World,
thanks to aviation pioneers like Clyde Cessna,
Olive Ann Beech and Lloyd Stearman. Clay
grew up on farmland outside the Air Capital
during the Great Depression, and it didn’t take
long for him to find his passion for flight. He
took his first flight on an airplane at age 8. By
age 12, he was working at a local airport in
exchange for flying time, and by 16, he was a
certified flight instructor.
At 19, Clay joined United Airlines as a DC–
3 copilot. He flew for United for more than 41
years and retired in 1992 as the airline’s most
senior pilot. He also served his country in the
California Air National Guard.
Clay’s leadership helped usher in a new era
for the American business aviation industry. In
1964, the first Learjet to touch down at Van
Nuys Airport was flown by Clay. Four years
later, he founded Clay Lacy Aviation, the first
executive jet charter company in the western
United States.
His impact on American aviation extends
beyond the cockpit. Clay helped develop
Astrovision, an air-to-air camera system that
changed how aircraft are filmed. His camera
system on planes captured aerial footage for
more than 2,000 projects, including the films
Top Gun and The Right Stuff. In 1988, he flew
a Boeing 747SP named Friendship One
around the world in just under 37 hours, raising more than $500,000 for children’s charities.
For more than seven decades, Clay has
logged over 55,000 flight hours on hundreds
of different aircraft types. He was enshrined in
the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2010
and inducted into the Kansas Aviation Hall of
Fame in 2011. Through the Clay Lacy Foundation, he has also helped young people pursue careers in aviation.
Clay has truly lived a life that advanced the
aviation industry, and his story began in the
Air Capital of the World.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of
Kansas’ 4th Congressional District, I want to

Lifetime Achievement Award and thank him for

Mr. COURTNEY. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to honor the life and legacy of an extraordinary Connecticut community member, Jere
‘‘Mike’’ Richardson, who passed away on October 12, 2026, at 86 years old.
Throughout his life, Mr. Richardson devoted
his time to the engagement and betterment of
his country and community. For example, he
honorably served our Nation in the United
States Army and the federal Environmental
Protection Agency, and on the local level as a
member of both the Lyme Land Trust and the
Old Lyme VFW. His attainment of excellence
in those endeavors made an indelible positive
impact, and he will be deeply missed by those
whose lives he touched.
Mike was born in Plentywood, Montana to a
family employed by and serving in the war effort in the 1940s. At an early age, Mike decided to step up and serve our country in the
United States Army and was nominated and
accepted into the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York. He graduated
first in his class in 1964, which given the high
level of West Point’s student body, is proof of
his exceptionalism.
While serving in the Army, Mike received his
master’s degree in engineering from the University of Illinois and was stationed in Thailand
where he aided the Royal Thai Air Force in
the development and construction of their runways.
After completing his military service, Mike
continued to expand his impactful and wideranging career. As an engineer in Seattle, he
contributed to the creation of the first tidal
aquarium in the world. After earning his law
degree from the University of Washington,
Mike moved to Washington, D.C., where he
returned to public service at the Environmental
Protection Agency, establishing the enduring,
groundbreaking concept of ‘‘you pollute, you
pay,’’ forever altering in a positive direction the
approach to environmental regulation in the
United States. Mr. Richardson then went on to
a new career as a lawyer for Pfizer in New
England, where he retired as the vice president of Environmental Health and Safety.
Mike Richardson made immeasurable contributions to his local community and to the
Nation as a whole. It is a privilege to share
some of his many accomplishments, and to
honor his service to our country. I had the
honor and pleasure to know him and his
amazing wife Faye Richardson over a number
of years, and benefited greatly from their
thoughtful, well-informed perspectives on
many issues and challenges our country has
confronted during my time in Congress.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the House to join me in
expressing our condolences to Mike’s wife and
high school sweetheart, Faye; his sons, Tom
and Pete, and their wives, Heather and Dass;
and to his nine grandchildren for their loss. His
legacy of deep intelligence, kindness, and integrity will long live amongst all of us who
knew him and be an example of a life well
lived.

HONORING THE 100TH ANNIVERSARY OF SOUTH JERSEY PORT
CORPORATION

HON. DONALD NORCROSS
OF NEW JERSEY

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

rfrederick on LAP6701GR3PROD with REMARKS

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Mr. NORCROSS. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to honor the 100th Anniversary of South Jersey Port Corporation. On Thursday, October
15, 2026, colleagues, friends, and members of
the community gathered at the Balzano Marine Terminal in Camden, New Jersey to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the South
Jersey Port Corporation.
Established in 1925 by the New Jersey
State Legislature and originally designated as
the South Jersey Port District and Commission, the entity expanded significantly throughout the 1940s and 1960s to support the region’s growing industrial needs. Renamed the
South Jersey Port Corporation in 1968, it has
since remained a cornerstone of economic vitality in Southern New Jersey and the broader
Delaware River Region, which was most recently exemplified by the opening of the
Paulsboro Marine Terminal in 2017.
For a century, the South Jersey Port Corporation has served as a catalyst for economic
development across seven New Jersey counties. Created to support a broad range of industries, the corporation today sustains thousands of well-paying union jobs across sectors
including steel, forest products, project cargo,
and manufacturing. The commodities moving
through its terminals supply essential raw materials and semi-finished goods that underpin
heavy
manufacturing
and
construction
throughout the United States.
At present, the South Jersey Port Corporation stands as a vital gateway linking global
markets with the Mid-Atlantic and the North
American heartland. For more than 100 years,
it has been a trusted leader in bulk, breakbulk,
and project cargo, facilitating efficient trade
flows with partners across Africa, Asia, South
America, and Europe while providing immediate access to more than 38 million American
consumers. The corporation continues to advance key initiatives; among them enhanced
rail connectivity, cleaner and more efficient
equipment, modernized terminal infrastructure,
and new avenues for cargo expansion, while
maintaining strong union employment and fostering workforce development.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully request that you
join me in recognizing and commending the
100th anniversary of the South Jersey Port
Corporation, an institution that has long demonstrated its dedication to both our Nation and
the Southern New Jersey region.

we celebrate 70 years of partnership, commitment, and love. They celebrated this incredible
milestone surrounded by their friends, family,
and loved ones at the Encinitas Community
Center.
On this special occasion, I extend my heartfelt congratulations and best wishes for continued health, happiness, and cherished memories.

RECOGNIZING AN OUTSTANDING
PUBLIC SERVANT AND THE HISTORICAL CAREER OF RETIRED
CRIMINAL
JUDGE
MIRIAM
WALTZER

HON. TROY A. CARTER
OF LOUISIANA

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to honor a remarkable and resilient
individual, retired criminal judge Miriam Waltzer. Born in Germany, she endured the tumult
of World War II, finding refuge in a convent
during the Holocaust. Her life took a turn for
the better when she met an American soldier,
leading her to the United States. Her journey
continued when she married Bruce Waltzer, a
civil rights lawyer, and she embarked on a
path toward justice.
Even though she had not completed high
school, given her husband’s background, she
gravitated toward a career in justice. Mrs.
Waltzer earned her undergraduate degree
from Loyola University, New Orleans, and her
Juris Doctorate from Loyola School of Law,
where she was one of only five women in her
law school class.
After graduating from Law School, Judge
Waltzer was the first woman elected Judge in
the Criminal District Court for the Parish of Orleans, Section ‘‘A,’’ in 1982. She served there
until 1992. She was then elected to the Fourth
Circuit Court of Appeal, Division ‘‘B.’’ She retired from that position in 2002.
Judge Miriam Waltzer, a product of oppression, was driven to improve the lives of those
in need. As a judge in Criminal Court, she
spearheaded programs to empower system-involved youth, fostering their connections to the
community and promoting their success in
school and life. She championed legislative reforms and advocated for the rights and protection of youthful victims. Judge Waltzer was
more than a symbol of authority. She was a
catalyst for change, advocating for education
over imprisonment for young offenders, and
demonstrating that toughness and kindness
can coexist.
Judge Waltzer has been honored numerous
times, both professionally and civically, for her

E:\CR\FM\A10NO8.049

E10NOPT1

E1192

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

many endeavors to benefit her profession and
the beloved City of New Orleans, which she
called home and its children. During her tenure, Judge Waltzer recognized the shifting demographics of defendants, with many becoming younger and less educated. She saw an
opportunity to make a difference in their lives,
offering probation with education as a key
component. Her belief in second chances was
palpable, and it resonated deeply with me.
I am honored to document the incredible career of retired Judge Miriam Waltzer as the
Orleans Parish Criminal Court celebrates the
official unveiling of the portrait and plaque of
Judge Miriam Waltzer that will forever be on
display in Section A of the Orleans Parish
Criminal Court building.
I am also honored to have witnessed her
courageous efforts during my career as a
member of the Louisiana House of Representatives, New Orleans City Council, and Louisiana State Senate. I am often reminded of all
the programs she created in the court system
as a Member of Congress. So many people’s
lives are forever changed because of the fight
she endured during her lifetime.

District Hospital Board, the Tulare County

Foundation, the Porterville Chamber of Commerce, and as Director of the Porterville Fair,

Brookshire to create Reed, Shoemaker,

REPUBLICAN VOTE TO BLOCK SEC.
HEGSETH’S IMPEACHMENT

HON. BETTY McCOLLUM
OF MINNESOTA

Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Ms. MCCOLLUM. Mr. Speaker, today,
House Republicans voted to refer articles of
impeachment against Secretary of Defense
Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee instead of
allowing a vote on the floor. This vote is another attempt by Republicans to shield Secretary Hegseth from the accountability Americans deserve. Since Hegseth’s nomination by
President Trump, I have stated concerns that
he was ill-prepared and not fit to serve as
Secretary of Defense, and questioned Trump’s
judgement in nominating him. Sadly, these
concerns were justified.
Mr. Hegseth swore an oath to support and
defend the Constitution of the United States,
he has willfully disregarded his responsibility
to faithfully execute the laws of the United
States. His removal is long overdue, but Republicans have once again refused to hold him
accountable. Less than three months after his
confirmation by the U.S. Senate, I called on
Secretary Hegseth to resign for mishandling
classified information when he shared war
plans on a phone messaging application. His
tenure has been marked by chaos and cruelty,
which impacts our servicemembers most directly.
Secretary Hegseth’s prosecution of the War
in Iran is clearly in contravention of the War
Powers Resolution of 1973. Congress has neither declared war, nor passed statutory authorization, and the United States was not attacked by Iran. Secretary Hegseth’s actions
have left our servicemembers dangerously vulnerable and placed the United States in an expanding regional conflict. Hegseth has systemically dismantled the office and systems designed to mitigate civilian harm in hostilities,
and that he stated were ‘‘stupid rules of engagement.’’ His willful disregard for U.S. laws
is a clear demonstration that he is unfit to
serve. His reckless actions have contributed to
the horrific killing of civilians in Iran, including
at least 120 children. Secretary Hegseth does
not get to choose which parts of U.S. law he
wants to follow.
From the beginning, I’ve said that Secretary
Hegseth was unfit to lead our men and
women in uniform. As Secretary of Defense,
he has made America less safe through his
chaos and gross incompetence. Republican’s
refusal to stand up for our Constitution and the
rule of law is disgusting. When Democrats
take the majority in the 120th Congress, we
will hold Secretary Hegseth accountable for
his illegal actions.

printed pursuant to directions of the Joint Committee on Printing as authorized by appropriate provisions of Title 44, United
States Code, and published for each day that one or both Houses are in session, excepting very infrequent instances when
two or more unusually small consecutive issues are printed one time. ¶ Public access to the Congressional Record is available online through
the U.S. Government Publishing Office, at www.govinfo.gov, free of charge to the user. The information is updated online each day the
Congressional Record is published. For more information, contact the GPO Customer Contact Center, U.S. Government Publishing Office.
Phone 202–512–1800, or 866–512–1800 (toll-free). E-Mail, contactcenter@gpo.gov. ¶ To place an order for any of these products, visit the U.S.

payable to the Superintendent of Documents, or use VISA, MasterCard, Discover, American Express, or GPO Deposit Account. ¶ Following

the Congressional Record.
